steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our computer vision paper on exemplar-free class incremental learning, where we propose Task-Adaptive Saliency Supervision (TASS) to stop saliency drift. Cover the incremental learning setting, related EFCIL methods, the saliency drift problem, the three parts of our method, and our contributions.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- Static vs. changing world; catastrophic forgetting
- Class incremental learning and the exemplar-free setting
- Existing EFCIL methods
- Saliency drift and existing saliency regularization
- Our approach: TASS and its three components
- Contributions

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- Static vs. changing world
  - deep nets: state of the art on many vision tasks
  - but static world: well-defined, stationary tasks, all data in one session
  - real world: changing environments/distributions + computational burden of training large CNNs -> learn new tasks incrementally without catastrophic forgetting (cite)
- CIL and EFCIL
  - CIL (cite): add new classes to trained models
  - most CIL methods use memory buffer of exemplars (cite)
  - EFCIL: no data from previous tasks kept; more challenging; realistic (privacy, long-term storage restrictions)
  - no exemplars -> forgetting much worse
- Existing EFCIL methods
  - DeepInversion (cite): invert networks from random noise -> images as exemplars, mixed with current samples
  - SDC (cite): update class prototypes; semantic drift estimated with new data
  - representation learning methods (cite); IL2A (cite): better representations reduce representation bias on new tasks
  - self-supervised tasks: Barlow Twins (cite), rotation prediction (cite) -> stable representations, less forgetting
- Saliency drift
  - CNNs attend to discriminative features for their tasks
  - forgetting in EFCIL also from attention drifting to new-task-specific features
  - standard regularization does little against saliency drift
  - distillation on saliency maps of old samples (cite) -> impossible without saved samples in EFCIL
  - saliency distillation between current samples and previous task attention (cite) -> semantic gap between current and old classes
  - no saliency regularization -> attention drifts to background -> forgetting
  - plain attention distillation (cite): no plasticity, susceptible to attention forgetting (key factor of knowledge forgetting)
  - TASS: keep saliency on incrementally learned tasks (Section 4), plasticity + stability; improves many EFCIL methods (Figure 1)
- Three components
  - dilated boundary maps at intermediate layers: stop drift across object boundaries; focus on foreground, adaptive attention within foreground
  - task-agnostic low-level auxiliary supervision task: stability across tasks; related to EFCIL since classification helps localize salient areas
  - module injecting saliency noise into feature channels, network trained to denoise -> resists attention drift
- Contributions
  - (i) new insight into task-adaptive saliency supervision in EFCIL; negative effect of no/trivial saliency supervision
  - (ii) TASS, three components
  - (iii) easy integration: MUC (cite), IL2A (cite), PASS (cite), SSRE (cite) -> significant gains
  - (iv) outperforms all EFCIL methods and several exemplar-based ones on CIFAR-100, Tiny-ImageNet, ImageNet-Subset

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Deep neural networks get state-of-the-art performance on many computer vision tasks. But most of these tasks assume a static world, where the tasks are well-defined and stationary and all the training data is available in one training session. The real world has dynamically changing environments and data distributions, and this, especially with the computational burden of training large CNNs, has led to renewed interest in learning new tasks incrementally without catastrophic forgetting.

Class Incremental Learning (CIL) is a scenario where new classes can be added to models that are already trained. Most CIL methods use a memory buffer to store exemplars from past tasks. In this paper we look at Exemplar-Free Class Incremental Learning (EFCIL), a more challenging setting where no data from previous tasks is kept. This scenario is realistic and very interesting because of privacy concerns or restrictions on storing data long-term. But not being able to keep examples from past tasks makes the problem of catastrophic forgetting much worse.

Several recent works look at the EFCIL problem. DeepInversion inverts trained networks starting from random noise to generate images as exemplars, and it mixes them with the current task samples for training. SDC updates the prototypes of each learned class, based on the hypothesis that the semantic drift of classes from previous tasks can be approximated and estimated with new data. Other works propose representation learning methods to overcome catastrophic forgetting. As IL2A points out, learning better representations can reduce representation bias when they are transferred to new tasks. Adding self-supervised learning tasks, like Barlow Twins and rotation prediction, has also been proposed to get more stable representations and reduce forgetting.

- Saliency drift
  - CNNs attend to discriminative features; in EFCIL attention drifts to new-task-specific features
  - standard regularization does little against it
  - distillation on saliency maps of old samples (cite) -> needs saved samples
  - saliency distillation between current samples and previous attention (cite) -> semantic gap
  - no regularization -> drift to background; plain attention distillation (cite) -> no plasticity, attention forgetting
  - TASS: saliency on incrementally learned tasks (Section 4), plasticity + stability; Figure 1
- Three components
  - dilated boundary maps at intermediate layers -> focus on foreground
  - task-agnostic low-level auxiliary supervision task -> stability (classification helps localize salient areas)
  - saliency noise injection + denoising module -> resist drift
- Contributions (i)-(iv): insight; TASS; integration into MUC, IL2A, PASS, SSRE (cite); beats EFCIL and several exemplar-based methods on CIFAR-100, Tiny-ImageNet, ImageNet-Subset

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Deep neural networks get state-of-the-art performance on many computer vision tasks. But most of these tasks assume a static world, where the tasks are well-defined and stationary and all the training data is available in one training session. The real world has dynamically changing environments and data distributions, and this, especially with the computational burden of training large CNNs, has led to renewed interest in learning new tasks incrementally without catastrophic forgetting.

Class Incremental Learning (CIL) is a scenario where new classes can be added to models that are already trained. Most CIL methods use a memory buffer to store exemplars from past tasks. In this paper we look at Exemplar-Free Class Incremental Learning (EFCIL), a more challenging setting where no data from previous tasks is kept. This scenario is realistic and very interesting because of privacy concerns or restrictions on storing data long-term. But not being able to keep examples from past tasks makes the problem of catastrophic forgetting much worse.

Several recent works look at the EFCIL problem. DeepInversion inverts trained networks starting from random noise to generate images as exemplars, and it mixes them with the current task samples for training. SDC updates the prototypes of each learned class, based on the hypothesis that the semantic drift of classes from previous tasks can be approximated and estimated with new data. Other works propose representation learning methods to overcome catastrophic forgetting. As IL2A points out, learning better representations can reduce representation bias when they are transferred to new tasks. Adding self-supervised learning tasks, like Barlow Twins and rotation prediction, has also been proposed to get more stable representations and reduce forgetting.

CNNs naturally learn to attend to features that are discriminative for the tasks they are trained on. In EFCIL, catastrophic forgetting also happens because the model's attention to salient features drifts to features that are specific to the new task. Standard regularization approaches don't do much to prevent this saliency drift when new tasks are learned. One direct way to regularize saliency is to apply distillation on saliency maps of old samples. But in the EFCIL setting this is complicated because samples from previous tasks can't be saved. Another way is to apply saliency distillation between current task samples and the attention of the previous task. But this method suffers from the semantic gap between current and old classes when saliency consistency is enforced.

If there is no saliency regularization, attention may drift toward the background in future tasks, which causes forgetting. Also, just applying distillation on attention does not give plasticity and is susceptible to attention forgetting, which is a crucial factor of knowledge forgetting. Our Task-Adaptive Saliency Supervision (TASS) approach instead tries to keep saliency focused on incrementally learned tasks (see Section 4 for more details), while keeping its plasticity and stability. By supervising their attention, it improves many previous EFCIL methods and gives them higher performance, as shown in Figure 1.

TASS combines three components to address this problem. First, we use dilated boundary maps to stop saliency from drifting across object boundaries at intermediate layers. Saliency drift usually happens across tasks, so making the model focus on significant foreground regions with dilated boundary supervision makes it less likely that saliency shifts toward the background, and the model can adaptively choose attention areas inside the foreground that are relevant to the task. Second, to also make the model's attention more stable across tasks, we add a task-agnostic low-level auxiliary supervision task to the class-incremental framework. This task is closely related to our core EFCIL task, since image classification has been shown to help models localize the most salient areas in an image. Third, we propose a module that injects saliency noise into some feature channels and trains the network to denoise them, which helps the network resist attention drift across tasks even more.

The main contributions of this work are: (i) We give new insight into task-adaptive saliency supervision in EFCIL settings, and we show the negative effect of methods with no or trivial saliency supervision, which shows why our method is better and why saliency drift mitigation is needed in EFCIL. (ii) We propose Task-Adaptive Saliency Supervision (TASS), with three components that together mitigate the saliency drift problem. (iii) We show that TASS can easily be integrated into other state-of-the-art methods, like MUC, IL2A, PASS, SSRE, and gives significant performance gains. (iv) Our experiments show that TASS outperforms all existing EFCIL methods and even several exemplar-based methods on the CIFAR-100, Tiny-ImageNet, and ImageNet-Subset EFCIL benchmarks.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Deep neural networks achieve state-of-the-art performance on many computer vision tasks. However, most of these tasks assume a static world in which tasks are well-defined and stationary and all training data is available in a single training session. The real world consists of dynamically changing environments and data distributions, which – especially given the computational burden of training large CNNs – has led to renewed interest in learning new tasks incrementally while avoiding catastrophic forgetting [1,2].

Class Incremental Learning (CIL) [3,4] is a scenario that considers adding new classes to already-trained models. Most CIL methods rely on a memory buffer that stores exemplars from past tasks [5,6,7,8]. In this paper, we consider Exemplar-Free Class Incremental Learning (EFCIL), a more challenging setting in which no data from previous tasks is retained. This scenario is realistic and of great interest due to privacy concerns or restrictions on the long-term storage of data. However, the inability to retain examples from past tasks significantly exacerbates the problem of catastrophic forgetting.

Several recent works consider the EFCIL problem. DeepInversion [9] inverts trained networks from random noise to generate images as exemplars and mixes them with current task samples for training. SDC [10] updates the prototypes of each learned class, hypothesizing that the semantic drift of classes from previous tasks can be approximated and estimated using new data. Other works propose representation learning methods for overcoming catastrophic forgetting [11,12]; as pointed out in IL2A [11], learning better representations can reduce representation bias when transferred to new tasks. Incorporating self-supervised learning tasks, such as Barlow Twins [13] and rotation prediction [12], has also been proposed to obtain more stable representations and alleviate forgetting.

CNNs naturally learn to attend to features that are discriminative for the tasks they are trained to solve. In EFCIL, catastrophic forgetting also occurs because the model's attention to salient features drifts to features specific to the new task, and standard regularization approaches do little to prevent this saliency drift. One direct way of regularizing saliency is to apply distillation on saliency maps of old samples [14], but this is complicated by the inability to save samples from previous tasks in the EFCIL setting. Another is to apply saliency distillation between current task samples and previous task attention [15], which however suffers from the semantic gap between current and old classes when enforcing saliency consistency.

A lack of saliency regularization may lead to attention drifting toward the background in future tasks, causing forgetting. Moreover, simply applying distillation on attention [15] fails to offer plasticity and is susceptible to attention forgetting, a crucial factor of knowledge forgetting. In contrast, our Task-Adaptive Saliency Supervision (TASS) approach aims to keep saliency focused on incrementally learned tasks (see Section 4 for details) while maintaining its plasticity and stability. By supervising their attention, it improves many previous EFCIL methods, as shown in Figure 1.

Specifically, TASS integrates three components. First, we apply dilated boundary maps to prevent saliency drift across object boundaries at intermediate layers. Since saliency drift typically occurs across tasks, encouraging the model to focus on significant foreground regions through dilated boundary supervision reduces the chance of saliency shifting toward the background and lets the model adaptively select task-relevant attention areas within the foreground. Second, to also enhance the stability of the model's attention across tasks, we add a task-agnostic low-level auxiliary supervision task to the class-incremental framework; it is closely related to our core EFCIL task, since image classification has been shown to help models localize the most salient areas within an image. Finally, we propose a module that injects saliency noise into certain feature channels and trains the network to denoise them, helping the network further resist attention drift across tasks.

The main contributions of this work are: (i) We provide new insight into task-adaptive saliency supervision under EFCIL settings, and show the negative effect of methods with no or trivial saliency supervision, which illustrates the superiority of our method and motivates the need for saliency drift mitigation in EFCIL. (ii) We propose Task-Adaptive Saliency Supervision (TASS), with three components that combine to mitigate the saliency drift problem. (iii) We show that TASS can be easily integrated into other state-of-the-art methods, such as MUC [16], IL2A [11], PASS [12], SSRE [17], leading to significant performance gains. (iv) Our experiments demonstrate that TASS outperforms all existing EFCIL methods and even several exemplar-based methods on the CIFAR-100, Tiny-ImageNet, and ImageNet-Subset EFCIL benchmarks.
